overview: Anglo-Saxon is a collective label for several peoples and societies that developed in early medieval England. Migration across the North Sea, interaction with Britain’s existing population, competing kingdoms and Christian institutions shaped this history. A single name should not imply one unchanging people, kingdom or way of life across the entire period.

periods.title: Early settlements and skilled households
periods.summary: Settlements such as West Stow contained timber halls, smaller buildings, pits and traces of household work. Their archaeological remains reveal communities rebuilding and using places over generations, rather than a single founding event.

periods.title: Christian missions and royal conversion
periods.summary: From 597, missions from Rome and Ireland helped convert English rulers. Christian institutions developed within societies already divided among kingdoms, alongside the older Christian communities of Britain.

periods.title: Elite burial and long-distance connections
periods.summary: The early-seventh-century Sutton Hoo burial brought together Frankish gold coins and Byzantine silver vessels. Such objects illuminate elite access to distant goods and help establish the burial’s date.

periods.title: The Lindisfarne Gospels are made
periods.summary: The British Library dates the manuscript to around 700. Its decorated Latin Gospel text shows the skill and resources devoted to book production; later additions document its continuing use.

periods.title: Mercia under Offa
periods.summary: Mercia became a major power under Offa. Its prominence followed earlier Northumbrian dominance, showing that political leadership shifted among kingdoms rather than belonging permanently to one center.

periods.title: Viking conquest and West Saxon resistance
periods.summary: The Great Army’s arrival in 865 brought conquests across several kingdoms. Alfred’s victory at Edington in 878 and agreements with Guthrum helped preserve Wessex while Scandinavian power continued elsewhere.

periods.title: Old English added to a Latin book
periods.summary: Aldred added an Old English translation between the lines of the Lindisfarne Gospels and a note about its makers. These additions belong to the tenth century, long after the original manuscript.

periods.title: England in Cnut’s dominions
periods.summary: Cnut’s rule joined England to a wider Scandinavian monarchy. Political rule and cultural identity did not fit a simple division between an exclusively English population and an exclusively Danish one.

periods.title: Norman conquest changes the ruling order
periods.summary: William of Normandy defeated Harold at Hastings in 1066. Castles, a new ruling elite and changes in the Church helped impose Norman power, beginning a prolonged transformation of English society.

sections.title: What survives of houses and working spaces

items.text: At West Stow, rows of postholes outline timber halls, while smaller structures left rectangular hollows with posts at their ends. The remains reveal different building forms within an early medieval settlement. Reconstructed houses help test explanations, but they are modern experiments rather than surviving Anglo-Saxon buildings.

Burnt remains in West Stow’s building SFB 15 included loom weights lying on planks. Preserved timber helped support an interpretation of a suspended floor above the hollow. The combination of structural traces and working equipment challenges the older assumption that people simply lived and worked on the bottom of a pit.

West Stow also produced a clay heap and pottery-decorating stamps, alongside finished pots, worked bone and antler combs. These finds reveal production skills as well as objects brought into homes. Timber buildings themselves required repeated carpentry, repair and replacement, making woodworking another substantial part of village labor.

sections.title: Food and textiles in daily life

items.text: Animal bones from West Stow document sheep, cattle and pigs, along with fishing, wildfowling and deer hunting. Plant remains indicate cereals supplemented by gathered foods. Loom weights and other textile tools, considered together with sheep husbandry, support weaving as an important skill; surplus cloth exchange remains an interpretation.

A laboratory study identified impressions of hulled barley in West Stow’s Anglo-Saxon pottery, with less certain traces of other cereals. The marks formed when plant material entered soft clay before firing. They are small physical traces of contact between pottery manufacture and the plant materials handled in the settlement.

The study cautions that grain impressions cannot be converted directly into crop-production totals. Whole grains and flour leave different traces, and fruit, leaves or roots are less likely to appear in clay. The apparent dominance of barley in this evidence therefore does not establish an exclusively barley-based diet.

sections.title: Migration revealed without reducing identity to ancestry

items.text: A 2022 ancient-DNA study found substantial continental northern European ancestry among its early medieval English samples, alongside people with more local ancestry. Hatherdene Close in Cambridgeshire showed variation within one cemetery. The results support large-scale migration and interaction, while ancestry alone cannot identify a person’s language or political allegiance.

The researchers compared ancestry with burial furnishings. Women with continental ancestry were more often buried with goods in the sample, but weapon graves among men did not follow a simple immigrant-versus-local division. A sword or brooch therefore cannot by itself reveal a buried person’s birthplace or ethnic identity.

sections.title: Sutton Hoo and the reach of elite exchange

items.text: At Sutton Hoo, a purse contained 37 Frankish gold coins, three blanks and two small ingots. The coins’ composition and minting dates help place the burial in the early seventh century. This is a closely studied elite assemblage, not a measure of how much money ordinary households possessed.

The burial also held a nested group of ten silver bowls identified as sixth-century Byzantine work. Their presence in an English grave shows objects traveling across great distances and remaining valuable over time. It does not establish a direct voyage by their final owner or identify every intermediary in their journey.

sections.title: Books as works of art and instruments of learning

items.text: The Lindisfarne Gospels, Cotton MS Nero D IV, combines Latin Gospel texts with decorated initials, Evangelist portraits, carpet pages and tables linking passages. The book required skilled work on parchment and careful organization. Its attribution to Eadfrith comes from a later note, so it is an attribution rather than a contemporary signed statement.

Aldred’s tenth-century additions placed Old English between the Latin lines and recorded information about the book’s makers. They show later readers using and interpreting an older object. Separating these additions from the original text reveals several generations of linguistic and religious work within one surviving manuscript.

Norman victory changed royal and ecclesiastical leadership and brought extensive castle and church building. It did not empty the country of its inhabitants. English and Norman communities interacted over subsequent centuries, while English continued to develop and eventually displaced French as the dominant language.

ending.text: The Norman conquest of 1066 ended the pre-Conquest English ruling order, with William of Normandy defeating Harold at Hastings. Communities and language continued under new rulers and changing institutions. Anglo-Saxon society was transformed rather than physically extinguished; the map’s 600 endpoint is only the end of this particular imported coverage interval.
